title: HPDT Nur23/599P — Tracy Moana Peterson (Nurses)
text:
BEFORE THE HEALTH PRACTITIONERS DISCIPLINARY TRIBUNAL
HPDT NO 1404/Nur23/599P
UNDER the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act
2003 (“the Act”)
IN THE MATTER of a disciplinary charge laid against a health practitioner
under Part 4 of the Act
BETWEEN A PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT COMMITTEE appointed by
the NURSING COUNCIL OF NEW Z
EALAND

Introduction
[1] A panel of the Health Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal (the Tribunal) convened via
audiovisual link on Monday 20 May 2024 to hear a charge laid by a Professional Conduct
Committee (PCC) of the Nursing Council of New Zealand (the Nursing Council) against the
practitioner, Ms Tracy Moana Peterson.
[2] The charge concerns 9 convictions entered in the Auckland District Court against
RN Peterson on 23 February 2023. The PCC alleges that these convictions are grounds for
discipline under section 100(1)(c) which enables the Tribunal to exercise its disciplinary
powers where the practitioner has been convicted of an offence punishable by 3 months’
imprisonment or more that reflects adversely on her fitness to practice.
[3] A full copy of the charge is attached to this decision as Appendix A. There are 6
convictions under section 249(1) of the Crimes Act 1961 of accessing a computer system for a
dishonest purpose and 3 convictions under section 228 of dishonest use of a document.
[4] Copies of section 249 and 228 of the Crimes Act 1961 are set out in Appendix B, attached
to this decision.
[5] RN Peterson did not dispute the charge. The onus of proof remains with the PCC and
the standard of proof is on the balance of probabilities.
Summary of findings
[6] The Tribunal finds that convictions as set out in the charge are punishable by
imprisonment for a term of 3 months or longer and reflect adversely on RN Peterson’s fitness
to practice. The provisions of sections 100(1)(c) and 100(2)(b) are met.
[7] The Tribunal orders the following penalty under section 101:
(a) Under section 101(1)(b), RN Peterson’s registration is suspended for a period of 6
months.
(b) Under section 101(1)(c):
3

(i) Within 6 months of her return to practice, RN Peterson must, at her own
expense, undertake and successfully complete a Nursing Council of New
Zealand approved course of study relating to ethics in nursing; and
(ii) For a period of 12 months following her return to practice, RN Peterson must
undertake professional supervision with a Council-approved supervisor for
12 months with reports each month to be provided to Nursing Council. The
purpose for this is for RN Peterson to engage with a professional supervisor
to discuss issues to ensure boundaries are not blurred in RN Peterson’s
professional nursing practice including an understanding that culturally safe
nursing care involves balancing power relationships.
(c) Under section 101(1)(d), RN Peterson is censured.
(d) Because RN Peterson is legally aided, no order for costs is made under section
101(1)(f).1
[8] Under section 95(2)(d) there is an order prohibiting publication of the name and
identifying details of the victim, [Mr N].
[9] The interim order prohibiting publication of the name and identifying details of the
practitioner continues for a further 21 days from the date of this decision, at which time the
order will lapse, but there is an order under section 95(2) suppressing references to RN
Peterson’s [childhood history].
[10] Under section 157 of the Act the Tribunal directs the Executive Officer:
(a) To publish this decision and a summary on the Tribunal’s website; and
(b) To request the Nursing Council of New Zealand to publish either a summary of, or
a reference to, the Tribunal’s decision in its professional publications to members,
in either case including a reference to the Tribunal’s website so as to enable
interested parties to access the decision.
1 Section 45(2) Legal Services Act
4

Evidence
[11] The parties filed an agreed summary of facts and an agreed bundle of documents. This
included a copy of the “Certified Copy or Extract of the Permanent Court Record” recording
the six convictions, as well as the Crown’s Summary of Facts which formed the basis of
RN Peterson’s guilty plea and sentencing in the Auckland District Court.
[12] It was agreed that RN Peterson is a registered nurse who holds a Bachelor of Nursing
qualification from the Manukau Institute of Technology. She was registered in the registered
nurse scope of practice on 13 December 2019.
[13] On 24 February 2023, RN Peterson declared to the Nursing Council that she had been
convicted of a criminal offence. She had initially entered not guilty pleas, but after a sentence
indication from Judge A-M Skellern on the morning of the scheduled trial, RN Peterson
entered guilty pleas to nine criminal charges.
[14] On the basis of the guilty pleas, RN Peterson was convicted in the Auckland District Court
of six offences punishable by a term of imprisonment not exceeding seven years, pursuant to
section 249(1) of the Crimes Act 1961 that she directly accessed a computer system and
without claim of right obtained a pecuniary advantage and/or a service. She was convicted of
a further three offences punishable by a term of imprisonment not exceeding seven years,
pursuant to section 228 of the Crimes Act 1961 that with intent to obtain any property, service,
pecuniary advantage or valuable consideration, dishonestly and without claim of right used a
document.
[15] RN Peterson was sentenced on 23 February 2023 and received 7 months of Home
Detention and reparation of $25,000.
[16] The Crown Summary of Facts included in the Bundle of Documents for the Tribunal’s
hearing sets out the circumstances of RN Peterson’s offending.
[17] At the time of RN Peterson’s court appearances, the complainant, [Mr N] was [age] years
old. He was described as a vulnerable elderly male who has had lifelong medical issues. He
had lived with his parents at their family home in [location] until their death. In 2008, after
5

the passing of his father, [Mr N]'s parents left him an interest in the house which he lived in
by himself from that point on.
[18] [Mr N] relies on daily in-home care for help with household tasks, showering, and
administering medication. Up until October 2019 his finances were overseen by The Public
Trust. He has lived a very modest lifestyle, with his spending primarily limited to groceries, a
prepay phone and minimal living expenses. He has not travelled outside of [location] for over
20 years.
[19] [Mr N] had set up two bank accounts through ANZ: an everyday “Freedom account” as
well as a “Serious Saver” account. He had a single ANZ bank card linked to his Freedom
account and did not use online or phone banking. He has never had a computer.
[20] In February 2019 RN Peterson, met [Mr N] through her mother [name], who worked at
a rest home where [Mr N] was a volunteer. RN Peterson befriended [Mr N]. [Mr N] considered
RN Peterson and her mother to be his friends. They both assisted him with home
improvements, driving him to various places and other everyday tasks. However, RN Peterson
and her mother were never employed as carers, nor were they paid for their assistance.
[21] Initially, RN Peterson reimbursed herself for legitimate expenses made to improve the
state of [Mr N]’s home. In the presence of [Mr N], she made online payments using [Mr N]’s
bank card and using the ANZ online banking platform.
[22] Between April 2019 and March 2020, RN Peterson used [Mr N]’s bank accounts to make
unauthorised bill payments, transfer funds to her own Kiwibank account and withdraw funds
for her own expenditure. She also made unauthorised transactions on his bank cards.
[23] According to the Crown Summary of Facts, the total amount taken by RN Peterson that
is outlined in the offences above was over $59,000. Reparation was sought for $54,605.24. RN
Peterson had declined to comment.
6

Charge 1.1: CRN 21004005344 - Accessing computer system for a dishonest purpose
[24] Between 28 May 2019 and 18 February 2020, RN Peterson accessed [Mr N]’s ANZ online
banking platform on 28 occasions and transferred a total of $17,900 from [Mr N]’s Freedom,
Select and Savings ANZ accounts to her own Kiwibank account. [Mr N] had no knowledge of
these transactions and did not authorise them.
Charge 1.2: CRN 21004005345 - Accessing computer system for a dishonest purpose
[25] Between 29 April 2019 and 28 May 2019, RN Peterson accessed [Mr N]’s ANZ online
banking platform and made four payments from [Mr N]’s ANZ accounts to Dental Care West
Ltd totalling $2,200. These payments were for RN Peterson’s own dental care treatments. [Mr
N] had no knowledge of these transactions and did not authorise them.
Charge 1.3: CRN 21004005347 - Accessing computer system for a dishonest purpose
[26] Between 24 May 2019 and 24 February 2020, RN Peterson accessed [Mr N]’s ANZ online
banking platform made 10 payments from [Mr N]’s ANZ bank accounts for flights with Air New
Zealand. These payments totalled $2,618.92. [Mr N] had no knowledge of these transactions
and did not authorise them.
Charge 1.4: CRN 21004005348 - Accessing computer system for a dishonest purpose
[27] On 12 July 2019 and 29 July 2019, RN Peterson accessed [Mr N]’s ANZ online banking
platform and made payments to Gurnell Harrison Stanley Law, located in Hamilton. These
payments were made from [Mr N]’s ANZ bank accounts and totalled $6,900.00. They were
made for legal services provided to a friend of RN Peterson. Gurnell Harrison Stanley Law did
not represent [Mr N]. [Mr N] had no knowledge of these transactions and did not authorise
them.
Charge 1.5: CRN 21004005349 – Accessing computer system for a dishonest purpose
[28] Between 16 September 2019 and 21 November 2019, RN Peterson accessed [Mr N]’s
ANZ online banking platform and made four payments from totalling $13,488.50, from [Mr
N]’s bank account to Nielsen Law located in Hamilton. They were made for legal services
7

provided to a friend of RN Peterson. Nielsen Law did not represent [Mr N]. [Mr N] had no
knowledge of these transactions and did not authorise them.
Charge 1.6: CRN 21004005576 - Accessing computer system for a dishonest purpose
[29] Between 25 November 2019 and 3 January 2020, RN Peterson accessed [Mr N]’s ANZ
online banking platform and made three payments from his bank accounts to Great Rentals
for rental vehicle hire. The payments totalled $473.00. [Mr N] had no knowledge of these
transactions and did not authorise them.
Charge 2.1: CRN 21004005574 – Dishonestly using a document – bank card 7791
[30] On 12 May 2019, a third ANZ bank account, a “Select” account, was opened under [Mr
N]’s name, using the ANZ online banking platform without [Mr N]’s authorisation. On the same
date an online request was made to ANZ for an Eftpos card for this account. This card ended
with the digits 7791, was embossed with the name “[Mr N]” and was mailed to [Mr N]’s home
address. [Mr N] was not aware of the existence of this Select account or the Eftpos card 7791.
[31] RN Peterson subsequently obtained possession of the Eftpos card 7791. RN Peterson
accessed [Mr N]’s online banking without authorisation and made multiple transfers from [Mr
N]’s ANZ Freedom account and ANZ Savings account into the newly opened ANZ Select
account. Between 1 October 2019 and 16 March 2020, RN Peterson used the ANZ Eftpos card
“7791” as her own. She made 63 purchases totalling $3,212.16 at shops around Auckland,
Whangarei, Gisborne and Wellsford. She also made 14 cash withdrawals, totalling $4,820,
from different ATMs around Auckland. These unauthorised transactions, totalling $8,032.16,
were all drawn from [Mr N]’s ANZ Select Account using the Eftpos card 7791. [Mr N] was
unaware of these transactions and did not authorise them.
Charge 2.2: CRN 21004501928 – Dishonestly using a document
[32] On 19 September 2019, another ANZ card was issued by the ANZ bank for the Select
account. This card ended with the digits 7092. RN Peterson obtained possession of this bank
card on various occasions between 29 November 2019 and 9 March 2020 and used the card
to make five Visa transactions for services including flights from Air New Zealand,
accommodation at Holiday Rotorua, and rental car hire from rentalcars.com, as well as
8

payments for “MIT grad” and ‘Academic dress”. The value of the unauthorised transactions
made using the card 7092 was $687.98. [Mr N] was unaware of these transactions and did not
authorise them.
Charge 2.3: CRN 21004501934 – Dishonestly using a document
[33] [Mr N] had a single ANZ bank card linked to his everyday Freedom account. The card
ended with the digits 1104. Between May 2019 and October 2019, RN Peterson obtained
possession of the bank card on various occasions and made 17 Visa transactions, for services
including dental care from Smilecare; flights from Air New Zealand; accommodation at The
Quadrant Hotel, Wairakei Resort, Holiday Inn and Lake Rotorua Hotel; and rental care hire
from rentalcars.com. The value of the unauthorised transactions made using the card 1104
was $2,304.68. [Mr N] did not give RN Peterson permission to use his bank card and did not
authorise the transactions that she made.
[34] It was further recorded in the Crown Summary of Facts that during the course of their
friendship, RN Peterson obtained an enduring power of attorney for [Mr N]’s property. This
was signed on 12 November 2019. RN Peterson engaged with Webster Malcolm Law, the law
firm in charge of [Mr N]’s late father's estate. Webster Malcolm Law could release funds to
[Mr N] when they were needed by him for legitimate expenses. Over 2019 and 2020 RN
Peterson continued communications with Webster Malcolm Law and on several occasions,
she tried to obtain further funds to be paid to [Mr N]. In February 2020, RN Peterson informed
Webster Malcolm Law that [Mr N] wanted to purchase a car and asked if they could release
money to pay for it. However, when enquires were made by Webster Malcolm Law they found
that the car in question was registered to RN Peterson, who owed a substantial amount of
money on it. This led staff at the law firm to become suspicious. They notified [Mr N] of their
concerns and reported the matter to Police.
Grounds for discipline
[35] The grounds on which a health practitioner may be disciplined are set out in section
100 of the Act. The relevant provisions of section 100 are as follows:
Grounds on which health practitioner may be disciplined
9

(1) The Tribunal may make any 1 or more of the orders authorised by section
101 if, after conducting a hearing on a charge laid under section 91 against
a health practitioner, it makes 1 or more findings
that
…
(c) the practitioner has been convicted of an offence that reflects
adversely on his or her fitness to practise.
(2) The Tribunal may make a finding under subsection (1)(c) only if the
conviction concerned
…
(b) has been entered by any court in New Zealand or elsewhere for an
offence punishable by imprisonment for a term of 3 months or
longer.
[36] Section 249(1)(a) of the Crimes Act 1961 (Accessing a computer system for a dishonest
purpose) carries a maximum penalty of 7 years’ imprisonment. Section 228 of the Crimes Act
1961 (Dishonestly taking or using a document) also attracts a maximum term of imprisonment
of 7 years. The convictions are clearly offences which qualify under section 100(2).
[37] RN Peterson accepted that these convictions reflect adversely on her fitness to practise
as a nurse. Both parties referred to settled law on this issue.
[38] The next question is whether the conduct reflects adversely on the practitioner’s
fitness to practise.
[39] At the time of this offending in 2019, RN Peterson was in her final year of study towards
her nursing degree, and in 2020 when the offending continued, she was newly registered.
Although RN Peterson described in her evidence that she assisted [Mr N] with getting up and
each morning and getting to bed at night, it was an agreed fact that she was not providing
therapeutic services to [Mr N].
[40] It is well established that the term “fitness to practise” extends beyond competence
issues. In Professional Conduct Committee v Martin2 Justice Gendall stated:
“Fitness” often may be something different to competence … aspects of general
deterrence as well as specific deterrence remain relevant. So too is the broader
2 Professional Conduct Committee v Martin CIV-2006-485-1461 (27 February 2007).
10

consideration of public or community’s confidence and the upholding of the
standards of the nursing profession.
[41] This Tribunal has on many occasions held that dishonesty convictions reflect adversely
on a practitioner’s fitness to practise. This has included cases involving fraudulent claims for
government funding,3 and theft from individuals.4
[42] The Tribunal has repeatedly made comments about the absolute requirement of
honest and ethical behaviour for registered health practitioners. There are many similar
quotes throughout the Tribunal’s decisions. In Murdoch Phys 06/45P5 the Tribunal said:
Fitness to practise cannot, in the context of a conviction, relate only to the
practitioner’s clinical ability. It must also involve a moral consideration and conduct
which offends the law or is immoral or unethical must reflect adversely on the
practitioner’s fitness to practise. Registration carries with it obligations to behave
in a way which is ethical, honest and in accordance with the law. Failure to uphold
the law or dishonesty must adversely affect a practitioner’s fitness to practise.
[43] And in Singh6 at paragraph [36]:
Honesty is a vitally important part of being a registered health profession for the
protection of the public safety and the maintenance of standards.
[44] In the Tribunal’s decision of Condon7 which concerned an enrolled nurse’s convictions
under section 228(b) of the Crimes Act 1961 the Tribunal said:
It is accepted by the Tribunal that any breach of trust and especially the dishonesty
offences for which Ms Condon has been convicted is conduct which must be
regarded as totally unacceptable behaviour for any enrolled nurse. It is also the
Tribunal’s view that members of the public are entitled to expect to be able to trust
and have confidence in the honesty of all members of the nursing profession.
Accordingly, the Tribunal believes that Ms Condon’s actions are ones that reflect
adversely on her fitness to practise in the wider sense, even if they did not occur in
the workplace.
[45] The Tribunal has no hesitation in finding that each of the 9 convictions entered against
RN Peterson reflects adversely on her fitness to practise. The offending was extensive. Each
charge is a “representative” charge. The Crown grouped the transactions according to bank
account or bank card. The Tribunal calculated that the conduct encapsulated in the 9
3 Murdoch 76/Phys06/45P, 19 December 2006; Winefield, 83/Phar06/30P, 5 February 2007.
4 For example, PCC v Condon 23/Nur05/13P, 12 January 2006.
5 Above, note 3 at [44].
6 475/Nur12/212P.
7 Above, note 4, at [37].
11

convictions involved over 130 separate transactions. Not only are they for offences involving
dishonesty, but the victim of the offending was a vulnerable, elderly man. The grounds for
discipline are established.
Penalty
[46] Having found the charge under section 100(1)(c) established, the Tribunal may consider
whether the conduct requires a disciplinary sanction for the purposes of protecting the
public and maintaining professional standards. Section 101 provides for the following
penalties:
(a) Cancellation of registration.
(b) Suspension of registration for a period not exceeding three years.
(c) Conditions imposed on practising certificate.
(d) Censure.
(e) Payment of costs of the Tribunal and/or PCC.
[47] The PCC sought a penalty of:
(a) Suspension of RN Peterson’s registration for a period of up to 6 months;
(b) Conditions with which RN Peterson must comply on return to practice;
(c) Censure.
[48] The practitioner accepted that a censure and conditions were warranted. Although she
conceded that suspension was likely, it was argued that a lesser suspension would suffice.
[49] In Roberts v Professional Conduct Committee,8 His Honour Justice Collins discussed
eight relevant factors in determining an appropriate penalty in this jurisdiction. These factors
have been summarised in the decision of Katamat v Professional Conduct Committee:9
8 [2012] NZHC 3354 at [44] to [51].
9 [2012] NZHC 1633.
12

(a) Most appropriately protects the public and deters others;
(b) Facilitates the Tribunal’s “important” role in setting professional standards;
(c) Punishes the practitioner;
(d) Allows for the rehabilitation of the health practitioner;
(e) Promotes consistency with penalties in similar cases;
(f) Reflects the seriousness of the misconduct;
(g) Is the least restrictive penalty appropriate in the circumstances; and
(h) Looked at overall, is a penalty which is “fair, reasonable and proportionate in the
circumstances”.
[50] The following guidance was also given in Katamat:10
In summary, the case law reveals that several factors will be relevant to assessing
what penalty is appropriate in the circumstances. Some factors, such as the need
to protect the public and to maintain professional standards, are more intuitive in
their application. Others, such as the seriousness of the offending and consistency
with past cases, are more concrete and capable of precise evaluation. Of all the
factors discussed, the primary factor will be what penalty is required to protect the
public and deter similar conduct. The need to punish the practitioner can be
considered, but is of secondary importance. The objective seriousness of the
misconduct, the need for consistency with past cases, the likelihood of
rehabilitation and the need to impose the least restrictive penalty that is
appropriate will all be relevant to the inquiry. It bears repeating however, that the
overall decision is ultimately one involving an exercise of discretion.
Similar cases
[51] There are many Tribunal decisions in which a nurse has been disciplined for convictions
of offences involving dishonesty. The parties referred to a number of cases, summarised below
in the order the Tribunal decided them.
[52] The enrolled nurse in Condon11 had her registration cancelled as a result of convictions
for one charge of dishonestly taking a document, namely an ANZ credit card and ten counts
10 Above, note 9 at [53].
11 See note 4 above.
13

of dishonestly using that document for a total of $1,222.47. Ms Condon did not participate in
the disciplinary hearing.
[53] In Harrison12 a registered nurse was disciplined on several grounds, including a charge
of professional misconduct for use of an ATM card belonging to a long-term patient at the
hospital where Ms Harrison was employed. The total amount of funds used came to $423.73.
For this charge and others of making a false declaration to the Nursing Council, and making a
false declaration to a prospective employer, the practitioner’s registration was cancelled and
she was censured. In this case, the practitioner did not seek to practise again.
[54] In Lal13 an enrolled nurse was convicted of two charges of dishonestly and without claim
or right, using a document with intent to obtain a pecuniary advantage. Both convictions
related to the use of money cards belonging to patients. The practitioner was censured, her
registration suspended for nine months, and conditions imposed on return to practice.
[55] The registered nurse in Griffiths14 was suspended for six months, censured and had
conditions imposed on her return to practice. The qualifying offences were misappropriation
of $170 cash, an ATM card and a Super Gold Card from a patient.
[56] Tameifuna,15 Jacobs16 and Mafua17 were all cases where the charge was one of
professional misconduct rather than a conviction.
[57] RN Tameifuna had stolen $70.00 from a resident. Her registration was suspended for
three months, and she was censured.
[58] RN Jacobs was found guilty of professional misconduct for taking a friend’s credit card
without authority and using it to purchase goods to the value of $3,598.00. She was
suspended for 9 months and conditions imposed.
[59] RN Mafua removed a patient’s credit card from their wallet, which had been left
unattended in a doctor’s room during her appointment and used it to pay an internet bill in
12 867/Nur16/364P, December 2016.
13 1129/Nur20/478P, 9 December 2020.
14 332/Nur10/150P, 12 October 2010.
15 182/Nur08/93P, 1 October 2008.
16 721/Nur14/301P, 17 August 2015.
17 1267/Nur21/532P, 15 September 2022.
14

the amount of $95.09. RN Mafua also stole cash in the amount of approximately $90.00 from
the patient’s wallet. Ms Mafua called the patient and while she admitted using the credit card,
she denied to the patient about having taken the cash, and falsely attributed this to another
staff member. Ms Mafua also was also initially dishonest to her employer about her conduct.
Her registration was suspended for 6 months, conditions imposed, and she was censured and
fined $2,500.
[60] Vanveen18 is another case of professional misconduct relating to dishonesty outside of
the workplace by a registered nurse assistant. She was convicted in Tasmania of 20 counts.
Her engagement with the proceedings lapsed, probably as a result of health issues. The
Tribunal imposed suspension of 9 months, reduction of 3 months being applied to account for
a lapse of time from the date of hearing.
[61] Ms Woodhouse also referred to cases involving other practitioners outside the nursing
profession. In Kong,19 a medical practitioner was convicted on 16 counts of fraudulently
claiming capitation-based funding totally $183,000, the Tribunal censured the practitioner,
suspended him for 12 months and imposed conditions on his practice, taking account of the
rehabilitation steps he had taken, his expression of remorse and his guilty plea. The Tribunal
said that it must consider the need to rehabilitate and to impose the least punitive penalty in
all the circumstances. The Tribunal therefore considered the need to rehabilitate Dr Kong back
into practice so that he may serve the needs of the Chinese speaking community and therefore
opted for a shorter period of suspension.
[62] Wang20 concerned a midwife who was convicted of fraudulently making claims totalling
$74,991 from the Ministry of Health over a three-and-a-half-year period. The Tribunal
censured her and suspended her for four months, noting that she had already suffered a
period of suspension because of her 4 months’ home detention, entering a guilty plea at the
earliest opportunity, full reparation had already been made to the Ministry by the time she
was sentenced by the Court, three years had lapsed since the last offending and there had
been no further offending, despite her continued practice, she had no previous convictions or
18 252/Nur08/109P, 14 September 2009.
19 422/Med11/181P, 6 December 2011.
20 654 Mid 14/283P, 16 September 2014.
15

prior disciplinary matters and she was remorseful and demonstrated insight into her
offending.
[63] In Chiew21 a pharmacist was convicted of 130 charges arising from fraudulently claims
for approximately $220,000 funding for undispensed repeat prescriptions over a six-year
period. He was censured and suspended for 9 months with conditions on his return to
practice. The mitigating factors were his early admissions of wrongdoing throughout the
criminal process, full repayment of reparation, no previous instances of professional or
criminal wrongdoing, his financial responsibility for his young family, his demonstration of
remorse to the Tribunal and support from his employer.
PCC submissions
[64] The PCC acknowledged the following mitigating factors. RN Peterson:
(a) pleaded guilty to the criminal charges and is not defending the professional
misconduct charges.
(b) has already been punished by the criminal proceeding (receiving a Home
Detention sentence and Reparation Order).
(c) has fully engaged in the disciplinary process and has signed an Agreed Summary
of Facts.
(d) has a previously unblemished record as a nurse and positive character references
were submitted to the PCC during the investigation stage.
[65] Further, in sentencing, the Judge identified a clear nexus between the offending and RN
Peterson’s background and history.
[66] The PCC noted the blurring of boundaries between RN Peterson and the victim, and
which was identified in the Judge’s Sentencing Notes, and submitted conditions could look to
address these issues to adequately manage future public safety risks (as part of a rehabilitative
approach to be taken).
21 180/Phar08/95P, 20 September 2008.
16

[67] The PCC noted that usually in a case involving dishonesty, it would seek cancellation of
registration for cases, but submitted in this case the appropriate penalty would be a period of
suspension of 6 months; this is to mark the seriousness of the conduct and to protect the
public, but also to enable a rehabilitative approach to be taken. During submissions, Mr Davis
suggested the Tribunal could consider a lesser period.
[68] Secondly the PCC sought an order of censure to express the Tribunal’s strong disapproval
of and significant concern regarding RN Peterson’s dishonesty.
[69] Finally, the following conditions were sought upon RN Peterson’s return to practice:
(a) RN Peterson must undertake and successfully complete a Nursing Council of New
Zealand approved course of study relating to ethics in nursing, to be paid for by
RN Peterson, within six months of her return to practice; and
(b) RN Peterson must undertake professional supervision with a Council-approved
supervisor for 12 months with reports each month to be provided to Council. The
purpose for this is for RN Peterson to engage with a professional supervisor to
discuss issues to ensure boundaries are not blurred in RN Peterson’s professional
nursing practice.
(c) RN Peterson must disclose the Tribunal decision to any employer before
commencing work as a registered nurse for a period of 12 months following her
return to practice.
The practitioner
[70] RN Peterson gave evidence to the Tribunal. She is now 49 years old. Following her
registration in December 2019, RN Peterson has held a number of nursing roles, including two
Practice Nurse positions, a vaccinator, a hospital nurse role, involving her in preparation and
training around the COVID-19 pandemic, swabbing and administering the COVID-19
vaccination and training others.
[71] At the time of her convictions in February 2023, RN Peterson was a Māori Clinical Lead
at Te Whānau O Waipareira delivering kaupapa Māori mental wellness services based on
17

traditional Māori systems of psychotherapy and wellness methodology to whanau. Since April
2024, she has been a Rongoā Māori Practitioner at the Auckland City Mission.
[72] RN Peterson explained that [Mr N] used to volunteer at a rest home where her mother
worked. Her mother had known him for some years. Following a twist of his ankle in October
2018, [Mr N]’s health deteriorated, and he had to retire from his volunteer work. A needs
assessment following a further accident in January 2019 led to a recommendation of
residential care. [Mr N] did not want to go into care and RN Peterson’s mother arranged for
her to move in to take care of his personal cares. RN Peterson did not feel she had a choice.
[73] Initially RN Peterson she did not stay with [Mr N]. She visited in the morning and evening
to help with getting him up and back to bed. RN Peterson had a part-time job and was
studying. It was agreed that she would quit her job to provide full-time care. In exchange she
understood that [Mr N] would pay for the things she had been paying for and saving for.
[74] RN Peterson said that initially [Mr N] paid for everything using cash. She suggested using
his visa debit card and he would be able to track his spending on his bank statements, which
he had difficulty understanding. It was agreed that RN Peterson would help him set up internet
banking so that he could access his historical bank statements without incurring a fee. She
then helped him pay bills online. Sometimes she paid items when he was not present. She
said that at the time, she understood he had consented.
[75] RN Peterson said as part of their arrangement [Mr N] had agreed to take over her
monthly dental repayments. She also believed that he had agreed that she could transfer
funds to her own account to help pay for her own expenses.
[76] RN Peterson said that [Mr N] used his visa debit card to pay for some of her expenses,
including accommodation, car rentals related to study break trips and to attend a student
nurse conference, her nursing registration fees and her graduation regalia. Although [Mr N]
paid for the graduation regalia, the April 2020 graduation was cancelled due to COVID, and he
received a full refund. There was also a domestic flight to accompany [Mr N] back to Auckland
after they drove to RN Peterson’s mother’s family reunion in Woodville then a family holiday
in Gisborne.
18

[77] RN Peterson had [Mr N]’s eftpos card and would use it to buy things for him as well as
her own petrol and food. This continued until she had started work in February 2020.
[78] RN Peterson borrowed money for legal fees for a friend. The loan was to be paid by the
friend’s mother but that fell through.
[79] At the time of the Tribunal’s hearing, RN Peterson had paid $14,700 of the reparation,
leaving a balance of $10,300. She started making weekly payments of $50.00 on 7 April 2024.
[80] RN Peterson said that she takes full responsibility for her actions and is deeply
remorseful for the distress she has caused [Mr N] and her own whānau. She said that she
disagrees that [Mr N] did not have knowledge of the transactions, but she fully accepts that
she should have properly accounted for the money she spent and borrowed from him. At the
time, she did not fully appreciate the power imbalance between them, and she justified the
spending on the basis that she had spent over 2000 hours caring for him. She said that she
now knows that it was inappropriate and wrong.
[81] RN Peterson said that her experience within the criminal justice system has been
extremely traumatic, and she does not wish to go through anything like this again. As a result
of her convictions, she has struggled to find employment that requires Police vetting and will
no longer be able to enter the USA to visit her 4 children and 2 grandchildren.
[82] RN Peterson said that until recently her rent exceeded her income, and she has used all
her KiwiSaver for her living costs over the past 14 months.
[83] Since being convicted, RN Peterson has been diagnosed with [health condition] because
of [childhood history] that was triggered during her experience in the justice system. She has
been seeing a counsellor weekly for the past year and has developed a greater understanding
for her actions and beliefs and is actively trying to address the underlying causes.
[84] RN Peterson hopes to continue her career as a nurse and understands the professional
ethical obligations required of her. She understands that her convictions reflect poorly on her
fitness to practice but is very committed to upholding the highest standards of patient care
and trust.
19

[85] RN Peterson provided 7 character references from friends and colleagues. She was
described as a person of good character, spending countless hours serving her wider
community; loyal, reliable, kind, funny, trustworthy, caring, respectful and non-judgement,
with high moral standards; hardworking, compassionate, with a selfless work-ethic; caring and
giving; dedicated her life to supporting and helping others both through her mahi and her
spare time.
[86] For the practitioner, Ms Woodhouse submitted that a period of suspension is not
warranted for the following reasons:
(a) RN Peterson was not practising as a nurse at the time of the offending;
(b) A period of 16 months has elapsed between the convictions and the Tribunal
hearing, during which time RN Peterson has been unable to practise as a nurse;
and
(c) The blurred nature of her relationship with the victim differentiates her case from
the archetypal dishonesty/fraud cases.
[87] In mitigation it was submitted:
(a) RN Peterson accepts responsibility for her actions. She pleaded guilty to her
criminal charges and has fully cooperated with, and engaged in, this disciplinary
process.
(b) RN Peterson is very remorseful for her actions. She wrote an apology to the victim,
accepting the seriousness of her actions and expressing her regret over the impact
they had on him. This demonstrates her insight, and an ability to self-reflect.
(c) psychological report, prepared for sentencing, and authored by consultant
forensic psychologist, Sarah Bramhall, details that RN Peterson suffered
[childhood history], which has affected her [health]. Ms Bramhall believes that RN
Peterson’s background caused her to overidentify with the victim, resulting in her
overstepping boundaries. Judge Skellern, the sentencing Judge, agreed. He
considered that the “psychological report as a whole identifies a very clear nexus
between this form of offending and [RN Peterson’s] background.” Given this,
20

education and treatment would play a pivotal role (as they already have) in
equipping RN Peterson with the tools to prevent such incidents occurring in the
future.
(d) RN Peterson has learned a lot from her actions and through this process already.
Specifically, RN Peterson’s experience within the criminal justice system
uncovered [childhood history] which led to [health condition] diagnosis and
resulted in her seeking treatment. For the past year, RN Peterson has been seeing
a counsellor weekly, and this has helped her accept and deal with [childhood
history]. RN Peterson’s engagement in such therapeutic processes will ensure
similar behaviour never happens again.
(e) There was only one victim. There is no suggestion of a pattern of behaviour
directed at multiple people.
(f) While RN Peterson admits her actions, the context was that she assumed a family-
like relationship with the victim. Boundaries were blurred as he permitted her to
make legitimate purchases. As commented by the psychologist, the development
of RN Peterson’s strong attachment with the victim may have contributed to RN
Peterson overlooking his vulnerability and overstepping her role. Despite the
victim’s vulnerability, he evidently demonstrated sufficient mental capacity to
understand his environment and make decisions. His request that RN Peterson
give up her part time job to look after his affairs, and his acceptance of RN
Peterson’s voluntary care, which included intimate tasks, likely contributed to her
misperception of their relationship as a familial one.
(g) It was further submitted that RN Peterson’s actions must be considered from a
cultural perspective. The Te Ao Māori understanding of familial relationships
differs from the western view. Reciprocal obligations and collective responsibility
are emphasised in Māori culture, and this perspective reinforces the submission
that RN Peterson misunderstood the nature of her relationship with the victim,
rather than dishonestly taking advantage of him.
21

(h) RN Peterson was not practising as a nurse at the time of the offending. The
relationship was familial rather than professional.
(i) The court-appointed psychologist assessed RN Peterson as having a very low risk
of future dishonesty offending.
Discussion
[88] The Tribunal is not persuaded by Ms Woodhouse’s submission that a term of suspension
is not warranted. Cancellation or suspension has been routinely imposed in similar cases, and
for the following reasons, it is the appropriate penalty in this instance.
[89] Despite RN Peterson’s evidence about the circumstances of this offending, and
submissions made on her behalf, the Tribunal must deal with these convictions on the basis
of the wording of the charges and the Crown Summary of Facts. In particular, [Mr N] did not
consent to the appropriation of more than $54,000 of his money for RN Peterson’s use.
Although RN Peterson pleaded guilty to the offending, she did not do so until the day of the
trial and now she seems to offer a defence that she was not aware that [Mr N] did not agree
to her actions. That would suggest a lack of dishonest intent, but RN Peterson pleaded guilty
to and was convicted of accessing a computer “for a dishonest purpose” and “dishonestly and
without claim of right” using the bank cards as a document. The time for exploring RN
Peterson’s knowledge and belief when making online payments and using [Mr N]’s bank cards
was at the criminal trial, not once the convictions have been referred to the Tribunal. It is a
matter of record that RN Peterson has broken the law on multiple occasions when engaging
in dishonest behaviour.
[90] RN Peterson believed that she was in a familial relationship with [Mr N] and at the start
of her offending she was not a registered nurse. Those factors do not absolve her of ethical
responsibilities. The victim was a vulnerable, elderly man, dependent on her for assistance
with a number of matters, including financial administration and personal care. RN Peterson
took advantage of that vulnerability. It is concerning that someone in their final year of nursing
training where a component of her education would have been discussion of the Nursing
Council Code of Conduct was not more reflective of her obligations towards vulnerable
people, regardless of whether she considered them family.
22

[91] Most of the conduct occurred before RN Peterson registered as a nurse. Had these
convictions been imposed before she applied for registration, the requirements of section
16(c) of the Act would have to have been met. This section provides that no applicant for
registration may be registered as a health practitioner of a health profession if they have been
convicted of any offence punishable by imprisonment for a term of 3 months or longer and
he or she does not satisfy the responsible authority that, having regard to all the
circumstances, including the time that has elapsed since the conviction, the offence does not
reflect adversely on his or her fitness to practise as a health practitioner of that profession.
The Nursing Council would have been required to undertake a similar exercise to that of the
Tribunal.
[92] This is not a charge of professional misconduct under section 100(1)(a) or (b). The
Tribunal does not need to decide whether the conduct was unprofessional. In that sense it is
not relevant that the conduct occurred before RN Peterson registered as a nurse. Irrespective
of any standards expected of a registered nurse, the conduct was immoral. The fact remains
that these convictions arise from conduct that occurred during RN Peterson’s nursing training,
immediately before and after her registration and reflects adversely on her fitness to practise
as a nurse.
[93] The Tribunal acknowledges that RN Peterson is clearly regarded highly by her colleagues
and friends. References from her employers would have provided more reassurance about
her standing as a nurse. However, it is encouraging that RN Peterson is now engaged in
counselling to help her deal with past [childhood history], and this is very likely to support her
rehabilitation including in relation to this offending.
[94] The Tribunal accepts that RN Peterson has the potential to make a valuable contribution
to the nursing profession, particularly in the provision of health services to the Māori
community. However, the Tribunal considers she needs to develop a better understanding of
her obligations to the vulnerable.
[95] It is commendable that more than half of the reparation ordered has been repaid. The
Tribunal recognises that RN Peterson’s employment opportunities and therefore her earning
23

capacity have been limited since these convictions. In Wang22 all the reparation of nearly
$75,000 had been repaid by the time the midwife appeared in court for sentencing, but the
Tribunal decided that a suspension of 4 months was still warranted.
[96] The Tribunal accepts that RN Peterson has been punished by the District Court and it is
for that reason that Parliament has stipulated that no fine may be imposed by the Tribunal
where a practitioner has been convicted in the criminal courts.23 However, the Tribunal’s role
is different. The principal purpose of the Act is to protect the health and safety of members of
the public by providing for mechanisms to ensure that health practitioners are competent and
fit to practise their profession.24 The Tribunal considers RN Peterson has some more work to
do to fully understand why her actions reflect adversely on her fitness to practise.
[97] The Act does not allow the Tribunal to order conditions before return to practice unless
a practitioner’s registration is cancelled. One of the penalty principles summarised in
Katamat25 is that the Tribunal must impose the least restrictive penalty in the circumstances.
Cancellation has been imposed for similar offending, but not usually where the practitioner
has participated in the proceedings and shown potential for rehabilitation.
[98] An order for suspension reflects the seriousness of this conduct, allows further time for
RN Peterson to reflect on her conduct in light of the Tribunal’s decision, and is consistent with
other penalties and protects the public. A term of 6 months sits appropriately with the other
cases cited above and is the least restrictive in the circumstances. Accordingly, under section
100(1)(c) the Tribunal orders that RN Peterson’s registration is suspended for 6 months from
the date of this written decision.
[99] The Tribunal also agrees that conditions are required on RN Peterson’s return to practice
under section 101(1)(c). Despite having completed her nursing training only recently, RN
Peterson would benefit from further education and reflection on ethics. As she continues her
career as a nurse, she will encounter other situations in which she will need to be aware of
power imbalances and her position as a nurse. Although she was not practising as a nurse for
much of her time with [Mr N], she may well encounter other situations in which her status as
22 Above, note 20.
23 See section 101(2).
24 See section 3.
25 Above, note 20.
24

a nurse will place her in circumstances where she can easily take advantage of a situation,
even if she does not see the relationship as a professional one. Accordingly, within 6 months
of her return to practice, at her own expense, RN Peterson must undertake and successfully
complete a Nursing Council of New Zealand approved course of study relating to ethics in
nursing.
[100] The Tribunal also considers a term of professional supervision would benefit RN
Peterson. This will provide an extra support for her as she re-enters the profession. It is also
an opportunity to discuss blurring of boundaries, including any particular challenges that arise
for her as she navigates her role as a registered nurse including within Te Ao Māori. Therefore,
the Tribunal imposes a second condition that for her first 12 months on return to nursing
practice RN Peterson must undertake professional supervision with a Council-approved
supervisor for 12 months with reports each month to be provided to Council. The purpose for
this is for RN Peterson to engage with a professional supervisor to discuss issues to ensure
boundaries are not blurred in RN Peterson’s professional nursing practice, including that
culturally safe nursing care involves balancing power relationships.26
[101] Finally, as part of RN Peterson’s accountability to the profession and to the public, for a
period of one year, she must disclose the Tribunal decision to any employer before
commencing work as a registered nurse.
[102] A censure under section 101(1)(d) is also appropriate to mark the Tribunal’s disapproval
of RN Peterson’s conduct.
Costs
[103] Under section 101(1)(f) of the Act, the Tribunal may order that the practitioner pay part
or all of the costs and expenses of and incidental to any or all of the investigation or inquiry
into the subject matter or the charge, the prosecution of the charge and the hearing by the
Tribunal.
[104] Because RN Peterson is legally aided, the PCC sought no orders for costs. Section 45(2)
of the Legal Services Act 2011 provides that no order for costs may be made against an aided
26 See Nursing Council Guidelines on Professional Boundaries.
25

person in a civil proceeding unless the court is satisfied that there are exceptional
circumstances. Subsection (3) sets out the matters that may be taken into account in deciding
whether there are exceptional circumstances. The Tribunal accepts that none of those matters
apply in the present case and so no order is made under section 101(1)(f).
Name suppression
[105] The PCC applied for an order prohibiting publication of the name of the victim, [Mr N].
The practitioner did not oppose this.
[106] Having considered the public interest and the personal interests of [Mr N], the Tribunal
is satisfied that under section 95(2)(d) it is desirable to order non-publication of the name and
identifying details of [Mr N].
[107] RN Peterson did not seek permanent name suppression but asked for a continuation of
interim name suppression for a further 21 days. The PCC did not oppose this. Accordingly,
interim name suppression will lapse 21 days after the date of this written decision.
[108] After the hearing, the Tribunal also considered whether to suppress details of RN
Peterson’s [childhood history]. Counsel was approached for comment. Ms Woodhouse agreed
that would be desirable. PCC counsel were unavailable. In any event under section 95 the
Tribunal may make such orders of its own motion and has decided that it is desirable to order
non-publication of RN Peterson’s [childhood history]. Any references to that will be redacted
from the final decision.
Dated at Feilding this 21st day of June 2024
T Baker
Chair
Health Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal
26
